title: Automating support triage without losing the relationship
metaTitle: Support triage that still reaches a person
excerpt: Sort support mail into buckets you defined, and wake a person when the bucket is urgent. Do not let the tool answer, refund, or close the thread.
alt: A clothing shop with racks, rope-hung industrial lamps, and a mirror. Support triage is the floor: someone has to know which message cannot wait.
caption: The shop floor, where someone must know what cannot wait. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should support triage send automatically?
faqs.answer: A receipt that says a person will read the message and when, without answering the question. Anything that explains a bill, offers a fix, or promises a time you cannot keep is a reply and waits. Two messages that disagree are worse than a short silence.

faqs.question: Which messages should wake a person immediately?
faqs.answer: Ones you listed in advance: checkout or login down, a charge they do not recognize, a privacy or safety concern, or a current client with a same-day launch problem. Anger is not the same as urgency. Write the rules from events, not from tone.

faqs.question: Should the tool close quiet tickets?
faqs.answer: Close a thread when a person marks it resolved or the customer confirms the specific fix. Thanks in a message can still include an unresolved charge. Auto-closing those tickets creates a second, angrier contact.

markdown:
Support triage automation should sort an incoming message into a bucket a person already defined, and it should interrupt someone when the bucket is urgent. It should not answer the customer, close the ticket, or refund them. A wrong public reply is the failure that minutes saved cannot pay for.

Automate the handoff around the message, especially when it might be urgent. The machine may label, route, and draft. Keep a person on anything the customer will see beyond a receipt, anything that moves money, and anything you cannot undo, such as a public promise or a closed complaint. Compare minutes of sorting with minutes spent fixing a misroute or a bad draft.

## Urgent is a list you write first

Before a tool reads the inbox, write the list of messages that cannot wait until the next digest. Keep it short enough that the team agrees.

- The site, the checkout, or the login is down, or the customer says they cannot pay.
- A charge they do not recognize, a double charge, or a refund that was promised and did not arrive.
- A safety, privacy, or legal concern, stated in their words.
- A message from a current client about a launch that is today.

Everything else can wait for a working-hour queue: how-to questions, feature wishes, praise, and mail that is not yours. The workflow's first job is to tell those two piles apart and to wake a named person for the first pile. A label without a wake-up is a filing system. Urgent mail needs a person who will see it within the hour you have promised, including the hour you did not staff. If nobody is on duty, the honest receipt says when a person will be.

Do not let the model invent new urgent categories because the prose sounded emotional. Anger is not the same as a down checkout. A calm "I was charged twice" is urgent. Write the rules from events, not from tone.

## What the machine may attach to the message

On arrival, the workflow can do four things and then stop.

1. Store the message in the queue the team already opens, with the time.
2. Apply one bucket from the list you wrote, plus a one-line reason that quotes their words.
3. Attach the obvious record if you have one: the order number they typed, the account email, the last invoice. If the match is uncertain, attach nothing and say the match is uncertain.
4. Draft a reply that a person will edit, using a template for that bucket, without sending it.

The receipt, if you send one automatically, is allowed to be automatic only when it refuses to answer the question. "We have this, a person will read it, here is when" is a receipt. A paragraph that explains their bill, guesses their order, or offers a fix is a reply, and replies wait. Two texts, a receipt that guesses and a person who corrects it, are worse than silence for twenty minutes.

Show the bucket to the teammate as a suggestion they can change with one action. If they change it often, the rule is wrong. Fix the rule. Do not add a second model to "learn" from overrides until a person can say what the new rule is. Learning that nobody can read will drift, and the drift will hide an urgent message in the how-to pile.

## Drafts for the buckets you actually have

Write templates for the buckets that repeat. A how-to template points to the one page that answers the question, and it says what to reply if that page is wrong. A billing template asks for the last four digits or the invoice number if those are missing, and it does not confirm a refund. A "not our product" template is polite and short, and it does not speculate about whose product it is.

A person sends these. The check is whether the template matches the message. A how-to template on a double-charge is the misroute you are trying to make impossible. The queue should make the bucket obvious at the top of the draft so the sender sees the mismatch.

Leave a blank template for the messages that do not fit. A blank is a signal to write, not a failure of the tool. Forcing every message into a closest bucket is how a privacy concern gets a password-reset link.

The [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) from the W3C is a practical test for the reply you do send. The guidelines sit under four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. Support mail is understandable when it names the problem you think they have and the step you are taking. It should not rely on a screenshot alone. If you describe an error, say what happened in text. You are not certifying the inbox. You are refusing to send a customer a puzzle when they already have a problem.

## Money, public replies, and closing

Refunds, credits, cancellations, and "we will make this right by Friday" are payment or promise, and they are hard to undo. The workflow may draft the sentence a person has already approved as policy. It may not choose the amount, the exception, or the deadline. A person who knows the policy sends it.

Do not auto-close a thread because the customer went quiet or because a keyword looked like thanks. "Thanks, but I was still charged" is not a resolved ticket. Close when a person marks it resolved, or when the customer confirms the specific fix. A closed ticket that was not fixed becomes a second, angrier message, and the relationship is worse than if you had left it open.

Do not post the reply in public, on a review site, or in a community channel, without a person. Public is a different audience. A useful private explanation can be a leak or a fight when it is pasted under a star rating. The triage tool can flag that a message is public. The response stays manual.

If the message is from a client you are in a project with, route it to the person on that project, not only to a general support queue. A launch-day "the form is broken" that sits in a shared inbox until Monday is a triage failure even if the label was correct. The project owner is the urgent path.

Hanabi's [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) is a set of shipped products and sites, which is also a set of relationships that had to survive the week something broke. Triage is how that week stays a conversation instead of a script.

## Minutes saved against minutes of repair

Time a normal day of the old inbox. Include the re-reading of threads to find the urgent one, and the time a non-urgent question waited because everything looked the same. That is the chore.

Time the new day. How long to accept or change a bucket, and how long to send a checked draft? Then add the repair: a customer who got the wrong answer, a refund that was not real, an urgent note that waited. Repair minutes count fully. If they exceed the sorting you removed, turn off auto-drafts and keep only the urgent wake-up. A wake-up with no draft is a valid, smaller automation.

Track overrides. If one bucket is overridden most days, rewrite it or delete it. A bucket nobody trusts is noise, and noise is how urgent mail gets skimmed past.

For the first twenty urgent messages, a second person glances before the reply goes out if the reply promises anything. After the templates have been right, a single owner is enough. The blank-template messages never become "good enough to send unreviewed." They were blank because the rule did not fit.

## What you tell the customer about speed

Publish one sentence about when a person reads messages, and make the receipt repeat that sentence. Do not let the tool promise a faster window because the queue looked short. Queue length is not a promise. If you miss the window, a person says so. An automated apology that goes out while you are still silent is a second disappointment.

Do not ask the customer to restate the problem in a form if they already wrote it clearly. The triage can ask one missing fact, such as an order number, inside the draft a person sends. A portal full of required fields in front of a human is how people give up and write a public complaint instead.

Keep the buckets, the urgent list, and the templates in the same place as the queue. When you add a new product or a new failure mode, add the bucket on purpose. A workflow that "covers support" without a list will file the new failure under whatever sounds similar, and the similar bucket will be wrong.

Once a month, read ten closed threads and ask whether the template still matches the product. A new feature will produce a new question the old how-to does not answer. Update the template in the same week, or the draft will keep teaching the wrong click. That monthly read is part of the minutes, and it is cheaper than a week of corrections.

Hiring mail is a different pile, with a person on the other end who is not a customer but still deserves a true answer. [Automating hiring inbox without losing the relationship](/blog/automating-hiring-inbox-without-losing-the-relationship) is the next piece, because an application needs a first read, and a careless no is hard to take back.
